subject: Biology
description: Alimentary canal, enzymes, organs, absorption sites, common disorders

questions.stem: The longest part of the human digestive tract is the:
questions.explanation: Small intestine is ~6.5 metres long in adults — divided into duodenum (~25 cm), jejunum (~2.5 m), ileum (~3.5 m). Most chemical digestion and nearly all nutrient absorption happens here. Compare: oesophagus ~25 cm; stomach ~25 cm capacity; large intestine ~1.5 m. Surface area further amplified by villi and microvilli (collectively a tennis-court-sized surface ~250 m²).

questions.stem: Which enzyme present in saliva begins the breakdown of starch into maltose?
questions.explanation: Salivary amylase (also called ptyalin) — secreted by parotid, submandibular and sublingual glands — starts breaking starch into maltose in the mouth at slightly alkaline pH (6.7). Inactivated by stomach acid. Pepsin — protein digestion in stomach (active at pH 1.5-2). Trypsin — protein digestion in small intestine (alkaline). Lipase — fat digestion (pancreatic + lingual).

questions.stem: The largest internal organ AND the largest gland in the human body is the:
questions.explanation: Liver — ~1.5 kg in adults, occupies upper-right abdomen. Functions: bile production (emulsifies fats), glycogen storage, urea cycle, detoxification, plasma-protein synthesis (albumin, clotting factors). 'Largest gland' because it secretes bile (an exocrine secretion). Pancreas is the second-largest gland — both endocrine (insulin/glucagon) and exocrine (digestive enzymes). Skin is the largest organ overall but not internal.

questions.stem: Bile, which emulsifies fats, is produced by the liver and stored in the:
questions.explanation: Bile is continuously produced by hepatocytes, concentrated and stored in the gall bladder, then released via the common bile duct into the duodenum when fatty food enters (triggered by hormone CCK — cholecystokinin). Bile salts emulsify large fat globules into smaller droplets, increasing surface area for lipase action. Bile pigments — bilirubin (gives stool brown colour, yellow if excess = jaundice), biliverdin.

questions.stem: Where is most of the water absorbed during digestion?
questions.explanation: Most water absorption occurs in the large intestine (colon) — converts the watery chyme arriving from the small intestine into semi-solid faeces. About 1.5 L of water per day is absorbed here. Trap: many students assume 'small intestine' because nutrient absorption happens there — but small intestine handles the bulk of organic-nutrient and electrolyte absorption, while the colon's specialty is water + Na⁺ + K⁺ + bacterial-vitamin absorption. Diarrhoea = colon's water-uptake fails.

questions.stem: Hydrochloric acid in the stomach is secreted by:
questions.explanation: Stomach lining cells: (1) Parietal / Oxyntic cells — secrete HCl (pH ~1.5-2) and intrinsic factor (needed for vitamin B12 absorption in ileum). (2) Chief cells — secrete pepsinogen (inactive); HCl converts it to active pepsin. (3) Mucous cells — secrete protective mucus. (4) G cells — secrete gastrin hormone. (5) Enterochromaffin-like cells — histamine. HCl kills ingested microbes and denatures proteins for pepsin attack.

questions.stem: The vermiform appendix in humans is best described as a:

options.option_text: Vestigial organ that may serve as a reservoir for gut bacteria

questions.explanation: Appendix — a small (~9 cm) finger-like blind pouch attached to the caecum at the start of the large intestine. Once thought purely vestigial; recent research suggests it functions as a 'safe house' for beneficial gut bacteria — repopulating the gut after a diarrhoeal flush. Inflammation = appendicitis; surgical removal = appendicectomy / appendectomy. In herbivores like rabbits, it is large and helps cellulose digestion.
